title: How does the optimizer implicitly bias the model merging loss landscape?
claim: Individual hyperparameters show no clear trend, but reparameterizing by one unifying quantity reveals a non-monotonic optimum in outcome.
layout: 3 line-plot panels, left-to-right, final panel shows shaded critical-point band
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the y-axis, accuracy gain (%) of merged models over single models. The left panel plots gain against learning rate, with one green-shaded line per batch size (bs16 to bs256). The middle panel plots gain against batch size on a log2 axis, with one blue-green line per learning rate. Both show tangled, crossing curves with no clear pattern. The right panel plots gain against effective noise on a log axis, using the same learning-rate series as the middle panel. Its curves collapse into one inverted-U shape that peaks near a hatched gray vertical band labeled 'Critical point'. Markers differ by series, and shaded bands show variance. The eye goes first to the right panel's peak.
caption: Effective noise scale controls the effectiveness of merging. The $y$-axis reports the test accuracy gain of merged models over single models. In (left) and (middle), plotting batch size against learning rate (or vice versa) reveals no clear trend. When reparameterized in terms of (right) effective noise scale, the joint interaction between different components emerges.
abstract: Model merging combines independent solutions with different capabilities into a single one while maintaining the same inference cost. Two popular approaches are linear interpolation, which simply averages multiple model weights, and task arithmetic, which combines task vectors obtained by the difference between finetuned and base models. While useful in practice, what properties make merging effective are poorly understood. This paper explores how the optimization dynamics affect the loss landscape geometry and its impact on merging success. We show that a single quantity -- the effective noise scale -- unifies the impact of different optimizer components on model merging. Across architectures and datasets, merging success is a non-monotonic function of the effective noise scale, with a distinct optimum. Decomposing this quantity, we find that larger learning rates, stronger weight decay, smaller batch sizes, and data augmentation all independently modulate the effective noise scale and exhibit the same qualitative trend. Unlike prior work connecting optimizer noise to the flatness or generalization of individual minima, we show that it also affects the global loss landscape, predicting when independently trained solutions can be successfully merged. Our findings broaden the understanding of how optimization shapes the loss landscape geometry and its consequences for model merging, suggesting that training dynamics could be further manipulated to improve model merging.
